paragraphs.heading: The middle of the margin
paragraphs.text: A continental margin is the outer edge of a continent's crust, where it meets oceanic crust under coastal seas. It has three parts: the continental shelf near the shore, the continental slope, and the continental rise farther out. Together, margins cover about 28% of the ocean's area. The slope is the steep stretch in between the shelf and the rise.

paragraphs.heading: It starts at the shelf break
paragraphs.text: Close to land, the shelf is a fairly shallow and generally flat stretch of seabed running out from the coast. Its average angle worldwide is just 0° 07′, and it is usually steeper near the coast than near its outer edge. The shelf ends at the shelf break, where the angle of the seabed rises drastically, and that is where the continental slope begins. The slope can stand 1–5 km above the deep-ocean floor.

paragraphs.heading: Canyons cut into it
paragraphs.text: The slope often carries features called submarine canyons. These canyons frequently bite deep into the shelf, with walls that are close to vertical, and keep cutting the seabed all the way down to the abyssal plain. They are often V-shaped and sometimes widen out onto the shelf.

paragraphs.heading: Where the slope ends
paragraphs.text: At the bottom of the slope the angle drops suddenly, and the seafloor starts to flatten out toward the abyssal plain. That flatter zone is the continental rise, which marks the outermost part of the margin. So a trip from the beach to the deep sea passes from flat shelf, over the break, down the slope and onto the gentler rise.

paragraphs.heading: Steep margins and gentle ones
paragraphs.text: Margins come in two kinds, active and passive. Active margins usually sit at plate boundaries, with volcanoes and earthquakes, and the west coasts of North and South America are examples. They tend to be narrow from the coast out to the shelf break, then drop steeply into trenches. Passive margins, such as the East Coast of the United States, are much wider and less steep.
